question: On what date did the National Credit Act come into commencement?
answer:
According to the context, the National Credit Act, 2005 (Act No. 34 of 2005) had a general date of commencement of **1 June, 2006** [nca_act_34_2005, p.1].

However, different sections came into operation on different dates:
- Sections 1–11 (Ch. 1), 12–25 and 35–38 (Ch. 2, Parts A, C and D), 39–69, 73, 134–152 (Ch. 7), 153–162, 164–170 (Ch. 8) and 171–173 (Ch. 9) commenced via Proclamation No. 22 in Government Gazette 28824 [nca_act_34_2005, p.105-106]
- Sections 26–34 (Ch. 2, Part B), 67, 68, 70 and 72 also commenced via the same proclamation [nca_act_34_2005, p.105-106]
- Sections 60–66 (Ch. 4, Part A), 71, 74–88 (Ch. 4, Parts C and D), 89–123 (Ch. 5), 124–133 (Ch. 6) and 163 also commenced via the same proclamation [nca_act_34_2005, p.105-106]

For example, section 60 specifically came into operation on 1 June, 2007 [nca_act_34_2005, p.41], and section 70 on 1 September, 2006 [nca_act_34_2005, p.47].

question: Which section of the National Credit Act gives a consumer the right to challenge the accuracy of information a credit bureau holds about them, without charge?
answer:
Section 72(1)(c) of the National Credit Act 34 of 2005 gives a consumer the right to challenge the accuracy of information a credit bureau holds about them, without charge. 

Specifically, section 72(1)(c) states that "Every person has a right to challenge the accuracy of any information concerning that person...that is held by the credit bureau or national credit register, as the case may be, and require the credit bureau or the National Credit Regulator, as the case may be, to investigate the accuracy of any challenged information, without charge to the consumer." [ncr_guideline_disputed_credit_complaints, p.2-3]

question: Both Directive D3/2023 and the IFRS 9 project summary describe a shift from an 'incurred loss' model to a forward-looking model. What is that forward-looking model called?
answer:
The forward-looking model is called the **Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model**.

Under IAS 39, the incurred loss model required a loss event to occur prior to a provision being raised [sarb_d3_2023_accounting_provisions_ifrs9, p.1]. IFRS 9 introduced the concept of ECL, requiring entities to "take into account all information that is available without undue cost or effort, including that which is forward-looking when determining impairments to be raised" [sarb_d3_2023_accounting_provisions_ifrs9, p.1].

The IFRS 9 project summary confirms this, stating that IFRS 9 implements "a forward-looking expected credit loss model that will result in more timely recognition of loan losses and is a single model that is applicable to all financial instruments subject to impairment accounting" [ifrs9_project_summary_2014, p.2]. Under this model, "an entity is required to recognise expected credit losses at all times and to update the amount of expected credit losses recognised at each reporting date to reflect changes in the credit risk of financial instruments" [ifrs9_project_summary_2014, p.14].

question: How did the FSCA's 2019 intermediary activity segmentation update build on the 2014 Retail Distribution Review?
answer:
The 2019 intermediary activity segmentation update built on the 2014 Retail Distribution Review in several ways:

**Foundation from RDR:** The 2014 RDR proposed an activity-based approach to categorizing intermediary services, proposing to "clarify which services are provided to which party and what capacity an adviser or intermediary acts in when performing these activities" [fsca_rdr_2014, p.3-5]. It outlined a framework distinguishing between advice, intermediary services, and other services provided to product suppliers.

**Operationalizing RDR proposals:** The 2019 segmentation work took this conceptual framework and implemented it with greater granularity. The FSCA and industry "carried out detailed technical work to determine the types of activities for which intermediaries are currently remunerated" and developed "a draft intermediary activity segmentation framework (segmentation framework) relating to activities performed within the short-term insurance environment" [fsca_rdr_intermediary_segmentation_2019, p.2-3].

**Specific regulatory interventions:** The 2019 update translated RDR proposals into concrete interventions, including "the capping of the maximum binder fees that an insurer may pay to a non-mandated intermediary (NMI) that is authorised to render advice, at a certain maximum per function performed" and "the introduction of an insurer notification process to the FSCA" for various remuneration and outsourcing arrangements [fsca_rdr_intermediary_segmentation_2019, p.2-3].

The segmentation framework demarcated activities into five categories: advice, other services to the customer, true intermediation services, services to the insurer, and other services not previously addressed [fsca_rdr_intermediary_segmentation_2019, p.2-3].
